A2.text:
Aysel is fourteen. She lives in Baku with her parents and her grandfather, Rashid. Her school gave her a project: “Baku in 2050”. She had to write a prediction about the future.

“The future is easy,” Aysel said. “Flying cars, robot teachers and no homework!”

Her grandfather laughed. “Wait here,” he said. He went to his room and came back with an old notebook. “In 1986, my teacher gave me the same project. Look.”

Aysel opened the notebook. The paper was yellow. Rashid wrote about “Baku in 2020”. He wrote: “Every family will have a telephone in their pocket. People will see their friends on a small screen. Shops will be inside the computer.”

Aysel was surprised. “Grandpa, you were right! Did you have a crystal ball?”

“No,” he smiled. “I just watched the young people. New things always come. It is only a matter of time.”

Then Aysel read the last page. It said: “In 2020, cars will fly over the Caspian Sea.”

They both laughed loudly.

“Nobody can see everything,” Rashid said. “But you can shape the future a little. Write about the city you want.”

That night, Aysel wrote about clean buses, green parks and a sea with no rubbish. She did not write about flying cars.

words.phrase: came back with an old notebook

questions.q: What does Aysel learn from her grandfather's old notebook?
options: He was right about many things, but not everything
He wanted to be a pilot
questions.why: Most of his ideas came true, but the flying cars did not.

questions.q: When did Rashid's teacher give him the same project?
questions.why: “In 1986, my teacher gave me the same project.”

questions.q: Which of Rashid's ideas did NOT come true?
options: Seeing friends on a small screen
Cars flying over the Caspian Sea
questions.why: They laughed at the last page: “cars will fly over the Caspian Sea.”

questions.q: Aysel wrote about flying cars in her final project.
questions.why: “She did not write about flying cars.”

questions.q: Rashid says new things are “only a matter of time”. What does he mean?
options: They will surely happen, maybe later
questions.why: He means new things always come in the end.

questions.q: Why did Aysel change her project?
options: Her grandfather said she can help make the future she wants
Her teacher did not like it
Her mother wrote it for her
questions.why: “You can shape the future a little. Write about the city you want.”

B1.text:
Aysel, fourteen, had a school project that did not excite her at all: “Baku in 2050 — make a prediction.” She sat at the kitchen table and typed quickly. “Flying cars, robot teachers, no exams. Done.”

Her grandfather Rashid looked over his glasses. “That is not a forecast,” he said. “That is a cartoon.”

Aysel rolled her eyes. Sometimes the generation gap between them felt as wide as the Caspian. “Grandpa, you grew up without the internet. What do you know about the future?”

Instead of answering, he went to his room and came back with a thin notebook, its pages yellow with age. “School Number 6, 1986,” he said. “My teacher gave us the same project.”

Aysel began to read. Rashid had imagined that every family would carry a telephone in their pocket, that friends would talk on small screens, and that shops would move inside computers. “Typewriters will become obsolete,” he had written in careful blue ink.

“This is incredible,” Aysel said. “Did you own a crystal ball?”

“No. I just noticed that every innovation starts small, with a few curious young people. After that, it is only a matter of time.”

Then she turned to the last page: “By 2020, cars will fly over the Caspian Sea, and nobody will need to work.”

They laughed until Aysel's mother came in to see what was happening.

“So I got some things wrong,” Rashid admitted. “Nobody sees everything. But a prediction is not only a guess. When you write down what you want, you help to shape the future.”

Aysel deleted her first paragraph. She wrote about sustainable buses, shady parks along the Boulevard and a clean sea. Then she added one more line: “Grandpa says the flying cars are still coming.”

words.phrase: did not excite her at all

questions.q: What is the main point of the story?
options: Old notebooks are worth a lot of money
Rashid's old predictions teach Aysel how to think about the future
Aysel's teacher gives too much homework
questions.why: Reading his 1986 project makes Aysel rewrite her own.

questions.q: What did Rashid think would happen to typewriters?
questions.why: “Typewriters will become obsolete,” he had written.

questions.q: According to Rashid, how does every innovation start?
options: Small, with a few curious young people
questions.why: “Every innovation starts small, with a few curious young people.”

questions.q: Aysel's mother helped her write the project.
questions.why: Her mother only came in because they were laughing; the text does not say she helped.

questions.q: Aysel feels the “generation gap” with her grandfather is wide. What is a generation gap?
options: A long time between two visits
A mistake in a school project
Differences in ideas between older and younger people
questions.why: He grew up without the internet, and she thinks he cannot understand the future.

questions.q: Why does Aysel add the last line about flying cars?
options: She is joking kindly about her grandfather
She really believes they will come in 2050
She wants to make Rashid angry
questions.why: After they laughed together, the line is a warm joke.

B2.text:
Aysel had fourteen years of experience in ignoring advice, and she intended to use all of it. The project was called “Baku in 2050 — a prediction”, and by nine o'clock she had finished it in four lines: flying cars, robot teachers, no exams, unlimited Wi-Fi.

“That is not a forecast,” remarked her grandfather Rashid from behind his newspaper. “That is a utopia drawn by someone who wants to sleep late.”

The generation gap in their flat was a running joke. Rashid still printed his emails; Aysel had never seen a fax machine. “With respect, Grandpa, you grew up with three TV channels. What would you know about the future?”

He didn't argue. He disappeared into his room and returned with a thin school notebook, its cover soft with age. “School Number 6, autumn 1986,” he said. “Same project, different century.”

Aysel opened it, expecting to be amused. Instead, she went quiet. In neat blue handwriting, a thirteen-year-old Rashid had described pocket telephones, friends chatting through small screens and shops that lived inside computers. “Typewriters and phone boxes will become obsolete,” he had predicted, “and many jobs will disappear before new ones are invented — a disruption, but not the end of the world.”

“Okay, this is genuinely creepy,” Aysel said. “Where did you hide the crystal ball?”

“There wasn't one. I simply noticed that every innovation begins with a few curious people whom everybody else laughs at. Once they exist, it's only a matter of time.”

Then she reached the final page: “By 2020, cars will fly over the Caspian and nobody will need to work.”

The two of them laughed so hard that the neighbour knocked on the wall.

“So I wasn't a prophet,” Rashid admitted, wiping his eyes. “But that isn't the point of the exercise. A prediction is half guess and half decision. The people who write down the city they want are the ones who end up helping to shape the future.”

Aysel deleted all four lines. Her new version described sustainable electric buses, shady parks stretching along the Boulevard and a Caspian clean enough to swim in. At the bottom, in smaller letters, she added a footnote: “My grandfather insists the flying cars are merely delayed.”

words.phrase: not the end of the world

questions.q: What makes Aysel take her project seriously in the end?
options: Seeing how much her grandfather predicted correctly as a boy
questions.why: She “went quiet” reading his accurate 1986 predictions and rewrote her work.

questions.q: What did Rashid call Aysel's first version?
options: A utopia drawn by someone who wants to sleep late
questions.why: “That is a utopia drawn by someone who wants to sleep late.”

questions.q: How did young Rashid describe job losses?
options: As the end of the world
As something only robots would cause
As a disruption, but not the end of the world
questions.why: “...a disruption, but not the end of the world.”

questions.q: Rashid says people who write down the city they want help to “shape the future”. What does this mean?
options: Influence how the future turns out
questions.why: He means a prediction is also a decision that changes what happens.

options: She still believes everything her grandfather wrote
She is angry that cars do not fly
She is teasing her grandfather affectionately
She thinks her new project is weak
questions.why: “Merely delayed” is a playful joke about his one big mistake.
